question: Does the corpus consistently describe an agent reviewing its own work as sufficient quality control?

suggested_queries: agent self-critique or self-verification sufficient without human review
AI agent reviewing own code quality assurance limitations
self-review vs human-in-the-loop quality control AI agents
rounds.answer: The retrieved evidence does not support this claim. None of the supplied items describe an agent reviewing its own output as an adequate substitute for independent quality control; in fact, the one item that most directly addresses code review explicitly says the opposite. That evidence states that even frontier models 'can pretty much do anything, but you need to review the decisions,' implying human review is required rather than self-review being sufficient. Other items touch on related but distinct topics: post-training as a human/process-driven refinement stage for model quality (not self-review), a model organizing itself into departments including 'quality control' (described anecdotally, without asserting that this self-organized review was sufficient), a speaker's personal struggle with how to 'validate AI generated code' (implying this is an unsolved problem, not that self-review suffices), and human oversight mechanisms where people edit an agent's memory/context to keep it behaving consistently (again indicating external control rather than self-sufficiency). None of these items make or support the claim that an agent reviewing its own work is sufficient quality control.

rounds.answer: The retrieved evidence does not support the idea that the corpus consistently treats an agent reviewing its own work as sufficient quality control. In fact, the few items that speak directly to this point suggest the opposite: one source explicitly states that even with capable frontier models 'you need to review the decisions,' implying human oversight is still required rather than self-review alone (688db16e3). Another describes a workflow where a separate agent (not the same agent that did the work) acts as a 'reviewer agent' making recommendations and helping with debugging, i.e., a distinct review role rather than self-review (ea8750bb4). Similarly, one source describes a coding workflow where one agent builds a prototype and a different, later agent 'comes back and cleans up the code,' again separating the builder from the reviewer (045c60f18). Another source recommends running a 'sub agent code reviewer' before committing code, which is a separate sub-agent step rather than the same agent simply reviewing its own output (5f16431dc). Elsewhere, quality control is described as something humans retain control over ('control on the R&D side the quality level, which ones get released') rather than delegated entirely to agent self-review (15ec12e77). Several other pieces of evidence discuss related but distinct concepts—model post-training/alignment (602612e9d), an agent splitting into departments including 'quality control' (58d7d3dd9), and agents 'dreaming'/introspecting on past trajectories to self-improve (a3d6ead82, 7425f99a8, fe14e9d9e, 11c5afbe5, a38b1771)—but these describe self-improvement or organizational structuring, not a claim that self-review alone constitutes sufficient quality control. Taken together, the retrieved evidence leans toward describing additional review layers (separate reviewer agents, human oversight, or distinct cleanup agents) rather than endorsing an agent's self-review as sufficient.
